Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. I, um, I honestly wasn't sure if I should even make the appointment, because usually I try to just power through things, you know? But work has just been... well, I work as an information clerk, basically a receptionist at this big building downtown. The lobby has these really high ceilings, lots of marble and tile, so absolutely everything echoes in there. It's always busy, people constantly coming and going, deliveries, all of that. Usually, I don't mind it at all. I actually took a couple of communications classes back in college, so I generally really like talking to people and being right in the middle of the action. 

But lately, I just... I can't seem to handle the environment anymore. What really pushed me to finally call and come in today is that every single time a door slams—and they have these heavy glass doors that catch the wind and slam a lot—or even if someone just rolls a suitcase really fast across the lobby floor, I just jump. Like, I physically jump out of my chair. It’s like it’s happening all over again, and my brain just completely panics. And it’s not just a little flinch, either. It takes me a solid minute, sometimes longer, just to get my heart rate back down to normal. I just have to sit there gripping the edge of the front desk, trying to breathe, and I'm sure I look completely ridiculous to anyone walking by, but I just can't stop my body from reacting like that to every sudden noise.

I try to just focus on the voice on the phone, I really do, but that image just forces its way in.

Well, no, not exactly those feelings. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel intense fear or anger, or shame... definitely not shame, because I know I didn't do anything wrong. I was just doing my job, following the protocol we're supposed to follow when someone gets upset, which usually involves just listening and trying to de-escalate, but obviously, that didn't work with this guy. And I'm not really angry at him either, honestly. I mean, people get stressed, they snap, I get it. Working at a front desk, you see people at their worst all the time. Just last month, I had a woman scream at me because the vending machine on the fourth floor ate her dollar, like I personally control the snack machines from my computer. So, no, anger isn't really the right word for it. 

It's more just... it's that physical reaction I mentioned. That tightness in my chest. I try to meal prep on Sundays so I don't have to think about cooking too much during the week, just pop some chicken and rice in the microwave, maybe throw together a quick salad. \n\nAnd as for at night, I've always been a pretty heavy sleeper, thankfully. Well, honestly, that specific thing—the jumping at sudden noises—is actually what really pushed me to finally come in and make this appointment. I mean, my apartment is pretty quiet, but if I hear a sudden loud noise out on the street, I definitely flinch way more than I ever used to. 

But it is so much worse when I'm at the desk. Our lobby has these heavy glass double doors, right? And they're supposed to be on those hydraulic hinges that catch them before they close, but sometimes the wind off the street catches them just right, or a delivery guy kicks the stopper out, and the door just slams shut with this massive, echoing bang. Before this whole thing happened, I wouldn't have even blinked. I would just keep typing up my reports or sorting the mail. 

But now? Every single time a door slams like that, or even if someone just comes in and rolls a suitcase really fast across the lobby—you know those hard-shell carry-ons with the tiny plastic wheels that just clatter so loudly against the marble tile when people are rushing?—I just absolutely jump out of my skin. My whole body violently jolts, and for a split second, it's like my brain genuinely thinks it’s happening all over again. And even after I look up and see it's just a tourist or a FedEx guy, my heart is just pounding out of my chest. It literally takes me a solid minute or two of just sitting there, gripping the edge of the desk and taking deep breaths, just to get my heart back down to a normal rhythm. It's completely exhausting, to be honest, just feeling like my nervous system is constantly waiting for a loud noise so it can freak out.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because normally I'm a pretty easygoing guy. I mean, you kind of have to be in my line of work, right? You're dealing with the public all day, answering the same questions over and over—where's the restroom, what time is check-out, can I get extra towels—and you just learn to let it roll off your back. I've always prided myself on being really patient with people, especially my coworkers. We have a good team, and I try to be the guy who keeps things light, you know? 

But lately... yeah, I guess I have noticed a little bit of a shift. It's not like I'm flying off the handle or throwing things or getting into shouting matches. It's more just this... this low-level irritation that I can't quite shake. Like, just the other day, one of the newer girls at the desk—Sarah, I think she started maybe three weeks ago, sweet girl, still learning the ropes—she asked me to repeat a confirmation number for a guest. And normally, I wouldn't even think twice about it. I'd just read it back, no big deal. But for some reason, I just felt this sudden flash of annoyance, and I snapped at her. I gave her this really short, clipped answer, like, "I just told you, it's 4-B-as-in-Bravo-7-9." And the second it came out of my mouth, I saw her face kind of fall, and I felt terrible. 

And it's not just her. It's little things. Like if the printer jams, which it does constantly because it's this ancient machine they refuse to replace, I find myself muttering under my breath and slamming the paper tray back in way harder than I need to. Or if a coworker takes a little too long explaining something during shift change, I can feel myself just wanting to cut them off and say, "Yeah, yeah, I got it, move on." 

It's weird because, like I said, I'm usually pretty careful with my coworkers. We all have to work in this tight space behind the desk for eight hours a day, so you want to keep the peace. But it's like my fuse is just... shorter right now. I don't know if it's because I'm so exhausted from the jumping at noises and the chest tightness, or if it's just my brain being on overload, but yeah, I'm definitely snapping over stupid little things that never used to bother me. I actually ended up bringing in a box of donuts the day after I snapped at Sarah, just to kind of smooth things over, because I really didn't want her thinking I was a jerk. But it's definitely something I'm noticing, and I really don't like being that guy.

I try to just focus on the voice on the phone, I really do, but that image just forces its way in.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself thinking about that event when you're not at work, like during the day when you're doing other things or even when you're trying to fall asleep at night?\n\nPatient: Honestly, no, not really. It's funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day when I was on my way home. Once I clock out and actually leave that building, it's like a switch flips, you know? I take the train home, usually the Red Line, which is a whole other kind of stressful because it's always completely packed at 5:30 and you can barely find a place to stand, let alone sit. But I just put my headphones in, I usually listen to this history podcast I've been really into lately—it's about the Roman Empire, super fascinating stuff, they really dive deep into the day-to-day politics and infrastructure of it all—and by the time I get back to my apartment, I'm really just focused on making dinner. I try to meal prep on Sundays so I don't have to think about cooking too much during the week, just pop some chicken and rice in the microwave, maybe throw together a quick salad. \n\nAnd as for at night, I've always been a pretty heavy sleeper, thankfully. I actually bought this new memory foam mattress topper a few months ago because my old bed was getting a little lumpy, and honestly, once my head hits the pillow, I am pretty much out cold until my alarm goes off at 6 AM. So, yeah, when I'm at home or just out running errands on the weekend, going to the grocery store, doing laundry, whatever, I'm just doing my own thing. I don't really find myself dwelling on what happened with that guy. It's really just when I'm physically back in that lobby, sitting in that exact rolling chair, looking at that same marble counter, that it all kind of floods back into my head. But at home or trying to sleep? No, I haven't really noticed those thoughts popping up at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself avoiding anything at work or in the lobby because it reminds you of that incident with the guest?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, actually, I have. I mean, it's kind of hard to avoid the lobby completely since my desk is right smack in the middle of it, but I've definitely started changing how I move around the building when I'm not glued to my chair. Like, usually, if I need to run to the restroom or go to the break room to grab a coffee—we have this really nice espresso machine in there now, which is a lifesaver on Monday mornings—I would just walk right across the main floor. It's the most direct route, obviously. \n\nBut lately, ever since that whole thing happened, I've been taking the back hallway instead. It's this long, kind of dingy service corridor that the maintenance guys mostly use, and it smells a little bit like bleach and old cardboard, but I just... I find myself taking the long way around whenever I possibly can. Because if I try to walk past that specific spot in the lobby, right in front of the counter where he was standing when he lost it, my chest just gets incredibly tight. It's like this sudden, heavy pressure right in the middle of my ribs, and I get this overwhelming urge to just get away from that space as fast as humanly possible. \n\nI know it probably looks a little weird to my coworkers, seeing me pop out of the service doors instead of just walking across the floor like a normal person, but I just can't bring myself to walk through that exact area if I don't absolutely have to. It's just too much. I'd rather deal with the bleach smell in the back hallway than feel that tightness in my chest, you know?\n\nDoctor: When you're in that area of the lobby or thinking about the incident, do you find yourself feeling intense fear, anger, or shame about what happened?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not exactly those feelings. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel intense fear or anger, or shame... definitely not shame, because I know I didn't do anything wrong. I was just doing my job, following the protocol we're supposed to follow when someone gets upset, which usually involves just listening and trying to de-escalate, but obviously, that didn't work with this guy. And I'm not really angry at him either, honestly. I mean, people get stressed, they snap, I get it. Working at a front desk, you see people at their worst all the time. Just last month, I had a woman scream at me because the vending machine on the fourth floor ate her dollar, like I personally control the snack machines from my computer. It's like my body is just reacting on its own, completely separate from what my brain is thinking. So, yeah, I wouldn't say I'm sitting there feeling terrified or furious or anything like that. It's just that physical pressure and that urge to get away.\n\nDoctor: Since that incident, have you noticed yourself feeling more on edge or easily startled in general, even when you're not at work or thinking about the event?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly, that specific thing—the jumping at sudden noises—is actually what really pushed me to finally come in and make this appointment. I mean, my apartment is pretty quiet, but if I hear a sudden loud noise out on the street, I definitely flinch way more than I ever used to. \n\nBut it is so much worse when I'm at the desk. Our lobby has these heavy glass double doors, right? And they're supposed to be on those hydraulic hinges that catch them before they close, but sometimes the wind off the street catches them just right, or a delivery guy kicks the stopper out, and the door just slams shut with this massive, echoing bang. Before this whole thing happened, I wouldn't have even blinked. I would just keep typing up my reports or sorting the mail. \n\nBut now? Every single time a door slams like that, or even if someone just comes in and rolls a suitcase really fast across the lobby—you know those hard-shell carry-ons with the tiny plastic wheels that just clatter so loudly against the marble tile when people are rushing?—I just absolutely jump out of my skin. My whole body violently jolts, and for a split second, it's like my brain genuinely thinks it’s happening all over again. And even after I look up and see it's just a tourist or a FedEx guy, my heart is just pounding out of my chest. It literally takes me a solid minute or two of just sitting there, gripping the edge of the desk and taking deep breaths, just to get my heart back down to a normal rhythm. It's completely exhausting, to be honest, just feeling like my nervous system is constantly waiting for a loud noise so it can freak out.\n\nDoctor: Since that incident, have you noticed any changes in your mood or general outlook, like feeling more negative about yourself, the world, or the future, or having trouble experiencing positive emotions?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't think my whole outlook on life has changed or anything drastic like that. I'm not sitting around thinking the world is a terrible place or that everything is doomed. I still enjoy the things I usually enjoy, for the most part. Like, I still look forward to the weekends. I usually go to this local trivia night on Thursdays with a couple of buddies from college—we've been doing it for, gosh, almost four years now, and we actually won a fifty-dollar gift card to the pub last week, which was pretty awesome because their nachos are amazing. Like I said before, I know I handled the situation at the desk the best way I could under the circumstances. I followed the training, I didn't provoke the guy, I kept my voice level. I don't think I'm a bad person or bad at my job. \n\nHonestly, it's really just that physical reaction I was talking about. The chest tightness in the lobby and the jumping at loud noises. Outside of those specific moments, I feel pretty much like my regular self. I'm still watching my favorite shows—I just started rewatching that old sci-fi series from the early 2000s, the one with the spaceship that looks like a firefly, you know? It's still just as good as I remember. So, yeah, my mood in general is fine. I'm not depressed or walking around under a dark cloud or anything like that. It's just my nervous system that seems to be a little out of whack right now, not my actual personality or how I view the world.\n\nDoctor: Since the incident, have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or having angry outbursts, even about small things?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because normally I'm a pretty easygoing guy. I've always prided myself on being really patient with people, especially my coworkers. Like, just the other day, one of the newer girls at the desk—Sarah, I think she started maybe three weeks ago, sweet girl, still learning the ropes—she asked me to repeat a confirmation number for a guest. And normally, I wouldn't even think twice about it. I'd just read it back, no big deal. But for some reason, I just felt this sudden flash of annoyance, and I snapped at her. I gave her this really short, clipped answer, like, \"I just told you, it's 4-B-as-in-Bravo-7-9.\" And the second it came out of my mouth, I saw her face kind of fall, and I felt terrible. \n\nAnd it's not just her. It's little things. I actually ended up bringing in a box of donuts the day after I snapped at Sarah, just to kind of smooth things over, because I really didn't want her thinking I was a jerk. It's completely exhausting, to be honest, just feeling like my nervous system is constantly waiting for a loud noise so it can freak out.\n\nDoctor: Since that incident, have you noticed any changes in your mood or general outlook, like feeling more negative about yourself, the world, or the future, or having trouble experiencing positive emotions?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel intense fear or anger, or shame... definitely not shame, because I know I didn't do anything wrong. I was just doing my job, following the protocol we're supposed to follow when someone gets upset, which usually involves just listening and trying to de-escalate, but obviously, that didn't work with this guy. And I'm not really angry at him either, honestly. I mean, people get stressed, they snap, I get it. Working at a front desk, you see people at their worst all the time. I actually ended up bringing in a box of donuts the day after I snapped at Sarah, just to kind of smooth things over, because I really didn't want her thinking I was a jerk.
